question: Can a pretrained neural symbolic regressor be steered at inference time by user hypotheses about equation structure, constants, complexity, and symmetry, while retaining unconditioned performance and improving equation recovery under noise and scarce observations?

key_findings.claim: NSRwH adds test-time structural prompting to NeSymReS through a separate symbolic encoder whose output is fused with the numerical-set encoding before autoregressive equation decoding.
key_findings.evidence: Numerical observations and a token string of hypotheses are processed by separate five-layer set encoders. Both produce tensors of shape (B,50,512), which are added elementwise and passed to a five-layer Transformer decoder. The decoder produces prefix-notation candidates by beam search, after which BFGS fits placeholder constants. Masking most hypothesis types during synthetic pretraining is intended to preserve operation when some or all hints are absent.

key_findings.claim: The conditioning vocabulary is unusually broad for a 2023 pretrained neural regressor: exact complexity, generalized symmetries, present subtrees, absent subtrees, and known numerical constants can all be supplied without retraining.
key_findings.evidence: Complexity is a single token for expression length 1-20; symmetry uses positive and negative tokens for 25 informative variable subsets; appearing and absent prefix subtrees are sampled with inverse-length-squared probability; and known constants are passed through numerical embeddings with pointer tokens placed in the output expression. The full ground-truth expression itself is excluded from the positive-subtree pool.

anchors.section: A.2.3-A.2.5 Branches, constants, and worked example

key_findings.claim: The model clearly responds to the requested properties, but control is soft and can weaken as decoding breadth or the number of simultaneous hypotheses increases.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 2 shows the matching model near 95-100% for positive branches, complexity, and negative branches and roughly 90% for symmetry, while the unconditioned baseline is much lower. However, agreement with positive, negative, symmetry, and especially the combined 'all' condition falls as beam size grows; the authors attribute this to interference and selection of hypotheses more consistent with numerical data. The reported is_satisfied score averages property agreement across beam predictions rather than guaranteeing that the finally selected equation obeys every prompt.

key_findings.claim: Correct oracle conditioning substantially improves numerical equation recovery, with the largest gains from combining all available properties and in noisy or small-data regimes.
key_findings.evidence: In the noiseless Figure 3, the combined condition reaches about 82% is_correct on train_nc versus about 66% for the baseline, about 35% versus 23% on train_wc, about 49% versus 19% on five-variable equations, and about 62% versus 51% on AI Feynman. Figures 4 and 5 show a persistent gap as output noise increases and observations decrease. Figure 6 rises monotonically from roughly 0.2 to 0.7 on train_wc as the fraction of ground-truth subtrees and constants disclosed to the model increases.

key_findings.claim: The experimental gains quantify the value of correct privileged information, not robustness to ordinary scientific hypotheses that may be incomplete, uncertain, or wrong.
key_findings.evidence: For every main controllability and accuracy experiment, complexity, symmetry, present/absent subtrees, and constants are mechanically extracted from the known ground-truth equation. Positive subtrees can disclose a cumulative prefix length equal to half of that equation, while the 'all' condition combines these with exact complexity and symmetries. Although the introduction explicitly says hypotheses may be partially incorrect, the paper reports no controlled sign, subtree, symmetry, complexity, or constant corruption test and no abstention or conflict-resolution metric.

anchors.section: B.2 Amount of conditioning during testing

key_findings.claim: Randomized structural prompts can diversify search even without prior knowledge, but the paper equates candidate count with computational budget and does not measure actual inference cost.
key_findings.evidence: On the 14 black-box ODE datasets, 500 random positive conditions with beam size 10 obtain is_correct 0.35 plus or minus 0.06 and mean R2 0.86 plus or minus 0.05, compared with 0.23 plus or minus 0.00 and 0.74 plus or minus 0.05 for one unconditioned beam of 5,000. A beam of 10 scores 0.12 plus or minus 0.04 and 0.32 plus or minus 0.03. Both large searches emit 5,000 candidates, but 500 separately conditioned decoding calls need not have the same latency, batching behavior, or memory cost as a single beam; none is reported.

anchors.section: 3.4 What if no assumptions can be made? and Table 1

key_findings.claim: The study isolates the benefit of conditioning relative to its NeSymReS base, but does not establish state-of-the-art symbolic-regression performance.
key_findings.evidence: The experimental section explicitly chooses only standard NeSymReS as the reference and declines comparison with genetic-programming methods because those methods cannot be conditioned by the same property interface. It also does not compare contemporaneous stronger neural, planning, unit-constrained, or hybrid search methods. Consequently the main result is a controlled architectural ablation, not a leaderboard claim across symbolic regression.

key_findings.claim: The numerical-recovery metrics do not prove exact symbolic recovery, and the principal plots omit uncertainty over models, datasets, or training runs.
key_findings.evidence: An equation is labeled is_correct when numpy.isclose holds on more than 99% of 500 sampled evaluation points, not when a computer algebra system proves equivalence; R2_0.99 is likewise thresholded. For most experiments, the same input points are used both to fit BFGS constants and select a beam candidate, although separate out-of-domain points evaluate the chosen expression on the synthetic datasets. Figures 2-11 show point curves without confidence bands; only the random-prompt Table 1 reports variation over five runs.

key_findings.claim: The claimed general interface is demonstrated only inside a small, expensive, generator-defined expression language.
key_findings.evidence: Training uses 200 million synthetic equations and takes five days on three RTX 3090 GPUs. Expressions have at most five variables, prefix length 20, depth 6, one scalar output, and a fixed vocabulary of ten unary and four binary operators. Three test sets are generated from the same grammar; AI Feynman and 14 ODE datasets add distribution shift but still must be representable by that token vocabulary. No experiment adds a new hypothesis type or operator after training despite the claim that the property set can be easily expanded.

anchors.section: B Training details and C.1 Evaluation datasets

key_findings.claim: The appendix contains a material ambiguity in the synthetic constant distribution that must be resolved through code before exact reproduction.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix A.1 states that additive constants are sampled from U(-10,-10), which is a degenerate distribution always equal to -10, while multiplicative constants are sampled logarithmically from U(0.05,10). This may be a typographical error for U(-10,10), but the printed procedure is unambiguous and would substantially change the training distribution if implemented literally.

method.core_idea: Learn one conditional distribution over symbolic expressions that accepts both numerical examples and a structured hypothesis prompt, so users can steer a pretrained neural regressor at inference time instead of regenerating data or retraining for every structural prior.
method.mechanism: A large synthetic generator samples expression trees, evaluates them on randomly sampled supports, and derives property tokens from the exact expression. A numerical set Transformer encodes up to 1,000 input-output points represented as half-precision bit vectors; a second set Transformer encodes the property string. Their equal-shaped latent sequences are added and decoded autoregressively into prefix expressions. Beam search supplies candidates and BFGS fits placeholder constants. During training, each hint family is frequently masked, creating conditioned, partially conditioned, and unconditioned examples in one model. At inference, users can supply any supported subset of exact complexity, positive or negative generalized symmetry, appearing or absent subtrees, and pointer-valued constants.
assumptions: Useful domain knowledge can be translated into the model's fixed property-token ontology.
The user's hypotheses are sufficiently accurate; the main experiments assume every supplied hint is ground-truth-consistent.
The target equation lies within five variables, prefix length 20, depth 6, and the fixed operator vocabulary used in pretraining.
Synthetic expressions and independent uniform supports adequately train representations that transfer to scientific observations.
Elementwise addition of numerical and symbolic encodings preserves both modalities and resolves conflicts sensibly.
Property masking probabilities during training cover the combinations and missingness patterns encountered at inference.
A beam size of five is sufficient for most comparative conclusions once correct privileged information is supplied.
BFGS can recover the numerical constants associated with the decoded skeleton and its selection loss identifies the best candidate.
Numerical agreement on sampled support points is an adequate proxy for symbolic equivalence.
Candidate count is an adequate proxy for compute when comparing 500 conditioned beam-10 searches with one beam-5,000 search.

techniques.role: Encodes unordered numerical observations and structured symbolic hypotheses in separate networks before latent fusion.
Represents complexity, symmetries, present or absent subtrees, and known constants as a serialized prompt.
Randomly hides hint families so one model supports full, partial, and absent prior knowledge.
Binds a provided numerical constant to a pointer token that the decoder can place without expanding the vocabulary per value.
Supplies prefix branches that must be encouraged or discouraged, sampled with a bias toward short reusable fragments.
Generates syntactically structured equation candidates token by token with beam search.
Optimizes placeholder constants against observations and selects candidates by numerical loss.
Uses many randomly sampled positive prompts as an inference-time diversity mechanism when no trusted prior is available.
Tests predicted expressions on 500 points sampled from a wider interval and thresholds numpy.isclose agreement at 99%.

evaluations.setting: Four test sets aggregated across 300 no-constant synthetic equations, 300 constant-bearing equations, 300 five-variable equations, and AI Feynman, with clean and 1% noisy outputs
evaluations.metric: Fraction of beam candidates satisfying positive-branch, complexity, negative-branch, or symmetry prompts as beam size grows from 1 to 256
evaluations.result: Conditioned predictions match positive, complexity, and negative prompts at roughly 95-100% and symmetry around 90%, substantially above the unconditioned model; several properties and the combined condition decline at larger beams.
evaluations.baseline: A separately trained, architecture-matched NeSymReS model with no symbolic encoder.

evaluations.setting: Noiseless train_nc, train_wc, five-variable, and AI Feynman equations with beam size 5
evaluations.metric: is_correct: more than 99% numpy.isclose agreement on held-out numerical support
evaluations.result: Combining all oracle properties is best in every panel, at approximately 82%, 35%, 49%, and 62%, versus approximately 66%, 23%, 19%, and 51% for standard NeSymReS.
evaluations.baseline: Unconditioned NeSymReS plus separate single-property conditions.

evaluations.setting: The same four datasets with multiplicative Gaussian output perturbations at rho in {0, 0.0001, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1}
evaluations.result: Accuracy falls for every method, but combined correct conditioning maintains a substantial advantage through moderate noise; nearly all methods collapse at rho=1 except residual performance from the combined condition on some datasets.
evaluations.baseline: Standard NeSymReS and each individual property prompt.

evaluations.setting: The same four datasets with 10, 25, 50, 100, 200, or 400 observed points
evaluations.result: All methods improve with more observations, but combined conditioning retains the largest benefit at ten points and remains best across the sweep.
evaluations.baseline: Standard NeSymReS and each individual property prompt.

evaluations.setting: Constant-bearing synthetic equations with the disclosed fraction of positive-subtree length swept from 0 to 1 and known-constant probability swept from 0% to 100%
evaluations.result: Recovery rises monotonically from roughly 0.2 with neither clue toward roughly 0.7 when the full prefix-length budget and all constants are disclosed.
evaluations.baseline: Less complete combinations of the same two oracle hint families.

evaluations.setting: Fourteen ODE-Strogatz black-box datasets with no trusted prior and 5,000 total decoded candidates
evaluations.metric: is_correct and mean R2 over five runs
evaluations.result: Five hundred random positive prompts with beam 10 score 0.35 plus or minus 0.06 and 0.86 plus or minus 0.05, versus 0.23 plus or minus 0.00 and 0.74 plus or minus 0.05 for a standard beam of 5,000.
evaluations.baseline: Standard NeSymReS at beam sizes 5,000 and 10.

evaluations.setting: All clean, noise, and sample-count experiments repeated with thresholded R2 above 0.99
evaluations.result: The appendix reproduces the qualitative advantage of combined conditioning and the same degradation patterns under noise and scarce points.

evaluations.setting: Fully masked NSRwH versus separately trained NeSymReS across noise and input-point sweeps
evaluations.result: The curves are broadly similar, supporting no-hint fallback, although visible gaps remain on constant-bearing and five-variable cases rather than exact equivalence.
evaluations.baseline: The standard model without any symbolic encoder.

limitations: All main improvements use privileged information mechanically extracted from the ground-truth equation; the paper does not test imperfect, contradictory, or probabilistic user hypotheses.
Appearing subtrees can reveal half of the ground-truth prefix length, and exact complexity and symmetry supply additional oracle leakage, so gains do not estimate realistic elicitation cost.
Only an architecture-matched NeSymReS baseline is used; there is no comparison with GP, AI Feynman, unit-constrained, planning-guided, or stronger end-to-end symbolic regressors.
Training requires 200 million synthetic equations, three RTX 3090 GPUs, and five days, limiting accessibility and weakening the claim of low overhead when pretraining is counted.
The supported language is capped at five variables, prefix length 20, depth 6, and fourteen fixed operators.
Three of five test collections share the exact training generator and differ only by random seed or constant/variable filtering.
The property interface is claimed extensible, but no new operator or hint family is added after pretraining to test modularity.
Property adherence is averaged across all beam candidates and is not enforced in final numerical-loss selection.
Numerical closeness on finite support is not computer-algebra proof of symbolic equivalence and can misclassify coincident or domain-limited functions.
Most plots lack error bars, confidence intervals, per-equation results, or multiple independently trained model seeds.
The 5,000-candidate comparison does not report latency, hardware utilization, energy, or memory and therefore does not establish equal compute.
The appendix prints a degenerate U(-10,-10) distribution for additive constants, creating a reproducibility ambiguity.
There is no scientist user study, online hypothesis revision loop, or measure of the effort required to express a useful hint.
BFGS fitting and candidate selection use the same observed points for most experiments, with only the final equation tested on a separate support.
failure_modes: An incorrect positive subtree or constant can steer probability mass away from the true equation, with no calibrated mechanism to ignore the hint.
Conflicting hints can interfere in the additive fused representation, as already suggested by the combined-condition decline at large beam sizes.
The final BFGS-loss selector can choose a numerically better candidate that violates one or more requested properties because adherence is not a hard selection constraint.
Expressions outside the pretraining operator vocabulary, depth, prefix length, or variable count cannot be recovered regardless of the prompt.
Half-precision bit inputs and discarding evaluations beyond 65,504 or NaN can bias training against stiff, singular, or high-dynamic-range scientific functions.
BFGS can converge to a poor constant fit or use a spurious skeleton to interpolate the observed support.
A wrong exact-complexity token rules out simpler or more accurate hypotheses without any uncertainty interval around complexity.
Symmetry tokens derived or estimated from noisy data can be unstable, especially when the normalized gradient is near zero.
Randomized prompts may improve diversity while multiplying decoding latency and may generate redundant or mutually equivalent candidate pools.
A numerically equivalent equation on sampled points can fail outside the tested domain or differ symbolically from the scientific law of interest.
When no useful hints are available, the extra symbolic encoder offers no guaranteed accuracy gain and can trail the standard model on some appendix panels.
Users can encode a mistaken scientific theory as a strong prompt and obtain a clean, high-adherence but false equation.
reusable_insights: Separate observation encoding from hypothesis encoding so a scientific model can expose an explicit control surface without regenerating its numerical training representation.
Train with structured hint dropout to make one model usable under full, partial, and missing metadata.
Pointer tokens are an effective bridge between discrete equation syntax and user-supplied real constants.
Positive and negative subtree prompts form a practical middle ground between unconstrained decoding and specifying the complete equation.
Randomized control prompts can serve as a diversity operator, turning a conditional generator into a search ensemble even without trusted prior knowledge.
Report both adherence and recovery: a controllable model can obey a hint perfectly while becoming less accurate, or recover numerically while violating the hint.
Evaluate hint quality as an experimental axis, including correct, missing, uncertain, contradictory, and adversarial cases.
Make final candidate selection constraint-aware rather than measuring property satisfaction only across the preselection beam.
Use interval-valued complexity and constants when scientific knowledge is approximate instead of requiring exact tokens.
A modular prompt ontology should be tested by registering a genuinely new property after pretraining, not only by masking known properties.
Numerical equivalence tests should be paired with symbolic simplification and adversarial domain sampling.
Inference comparisons should report candidates, unique simplified expressions, wall-clock time, memory, and accelerator utilization together.
open_questions: How does NSRwH behave as each hint is gradually corrupted, and can it learn calibrated trust weights or abstain from following inconsistent priors?
Can hard constrained decoding guarantee subtree, unit, symmetry, or monotonicity requirements while retaining the neural model's speed?
Does conditioning still help when built on modern TPSR, RAG-SR, Sym-Q, or larger end-to-end symbolic-regression backbones?
Can natural-language scientific hypotheses be compiled into the token ontology with a verifiable provenance trail and uncertainty annotations?
What is the human time cost of creating hints, and does an interactive scientist-in-the-loop workflow outperform spending the same time or compute on search?
Can the model actively ask which constant, symmetry, branch, or complexity range would most reduce posterior uncertainty?
How does the approach scale beyond five variables, depth six, prefix length twenty, and the fixed elementary-function vocabulary?
Can hypothesis encoders be plugged in after pretraining so new property types do not require another 200-million-equation training run?
Would contrastive or gated fusion resolve the interference observed when multiple hypotheses are combined?
What fraction of numerically correct outputs are algebraically equivalent after canonical simplification, and how many fail extrapolation outside U(-25,25)?
Is randomized hypothesis search still superior when compared at equal wall-clock time and after deduplicating algebraically equivalent candidates?
Can executable unit, conservation, boundary, and asymptotic constraints provide stronger scientific guarantees than soft subtree prompts?
How sensitive are conclusions to independent pretraining seeds, synthetic generator choices, operator frequencies, and the apparent additive-constant typo?
Can a Bayesian version return a posterior over equations and hypothesis satisfaction rather than one selected formula?

competitive_landscape.title: Neural Symbolic Regression that Scales
competitive_landscape.relationship: NeSymReS is the direct architectural and data-generation foundation of NSRwH and the only model baseline used throughout the paper.
competitive_landscape.difference: NeSymReS conditions only on numerical samples and uses a synthetic generator to define its implicit prior. NSRwH's contribution is an explicit symbolic-hypothesis channel, constant pointers, and hint masking at the cost of a second encoder and another 200-million-equation pretraining run.

competitive_landscape.title: Symbolic Regression Driven by Training Data and Prior Knowledge
competitive_landscape.relationship: A preexisting evolutionary method incorporates desired model properties as formal constraints and optimizes both data fit and prior compliance.
competitive_landscape.difference: It checks constraints during per-task multi-objective evolution rather than prompting a pretrained neural generator. NSRwH offers much faster amortized inference and richer syntactic hints, but the 2020 paper refutes any field-wide claim that injecting user prior knowledge into symbolic regression was first introduced here.

competitive_landscape.title: Deep symbolic regression for physics guided by units constraints: toward the automated discovery of physical laws
competitive_landscape.relationship: Phi-SO is a contemporaneous deep symbolic-regression system that uses physical units as prior knowledge to restrict expression generation by construction.
competitive_landscape.difference: Phi-SO enforces one scientifically important constraint family as a hard grammar during task-specific reinforcement learning; NSRwH amortizes inference and supports several soft syntactic properties. Phi-SO is a stronger comparator for physical validity and noisy Feynman recovery, while NSRwH is more flexible and interactive.

competitive_landscape.title: Transformer-based Planning for Symbolic Regression
competitive_landscape.relationship: TPSR augments pretrained Transformer decoding with Monte Carlo tree search and accepts non-differentiable external signals such as accuracy and complexity at inference.
competitive_landscape.difference: TPSR uses online lookahead and objective feedback rather than a learned prompt encoder, so it is slower but can adapt search criteria without retraining. It directly competes with NSRwH on controllable complexity, robustness to noise, extrapolation, and integrating prior knowledge into decoding.

competitive_landscape.title: LLM-SR: Scientific Equation Discovery via Programming with Large Language Models
competitive_landscape.relationship: A later equation-discovery approach uses a pretrained language model's scientific knowledge to propose program-form equation skeletons and iteratively evolves them against data.
competitive_landscape.difference: LLM-SR accepts broad domain context and richer program structures instead of exact ground-truth-derived property tokens, but depends on a large general-purpose model and iterative search. It is the natural comparator for whether structured NSRwH prompts remain competitive once scientific priors can be expressed in language.

competitive_landscape.title: RAG-SR: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Neural Symbolic Regression
competitive_landscape.relationship: A current neural-symbolic-regression alternative that learns online without massive pretraining and combines evolutionary feature construction with retrieval-grounded generation.
competitive_landscape.difference: RAG-SR targets unseen functions and variables and reports comparisons across 25 algorithms and 120 tasks, while NSRwH emphasizes instant control of a fixed pretrained grammar. It is a stronger modern accuracy/generalization baseline but does not expose the same explicit hypothesis-token interface.

competitive_landscape.title: DrSR: LLM based Scientific Equation Discovery with Dual Reasoning from Data and Experience
competitive_landscape.relationship: DrSR explicitly derives structured descriptions such as monotonicity, nonlinearity, and correlation from data and uses performance reflection to revise equation proposals.
competitive_landscape.difference: DrSR closes the loop between data analysis and hypothesis refinement, whereas NSRwH assumes users already know exact properties and performs one-way conditioning. NSRwH is smaller and deterministic after pretraining; DrSR is broader but LLM-dependent and iterative.

competitive_landscape.title: Prior-Guided Symbolic Regression: Towards Scientific Consistency in Equation Discovery
competitive_landscape.relationship: PG-SR is a later direct prior-guided framework with executable scientific constraint programs and annealed constraint evaluation through warm-up, evolution, and refinement.
competitive_landscape.difference: PG-SR explicitly evaluates varying prior quality, noise, and data scarcity and claims a generalization argument from a reduced hypothesis class. NSRwH offers amortized prompt-conditioned generation but lacks wrong-prior robustness, executable checking, and scientific-consistency guarantees.

competitive_landscape.title: Language models guide symbolic equation discovery by controlling search
competitive_landscape.relationship: The newest close competitor assigns a language model the search-controller role: it chooses variables, operators, transformations, and depth while PySR enumerates, fits, and deterministically retains equations.
competitive_landscape.difference: LLM-PySR generalizes the control interface from fixed oracle-derived tokens to language-informed search configuration and reports 74 AI-Feynman equations plus real battery data. NSRwH is cheaper at inference after training and conditions each candidate distribution directly, but its fixed vocabulary and absence of strict downstream constraint checks now look substantially narrower.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors present NSRwH as a general recipe for adding explicit, user-defined prior knowledge to pretrained neural symbolic regression at inference time, allowing controllable complexity, symmetry, present and absent subtrees, and constants without retraining; they further claim that correct hypotheses improve recovery and can diversify search even when no trusted prior is available.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The dual-encoder prompting mechanism, constant pointers, mixed property ontology, and hint-dropout training form a coherent and useful addition to the NeSymReS family. The visual results support both soft adherence and large recovery gains when oracle properties are available. However, prior-guided symbolic regression predates this work, AI Feynman already exploited symmetry and modularity, and contemporaneous Phi-SO and TPSR offered hard physical constraints or search-time objectives. The evaluation never supplies an incorrect hypothesis despite explicitly motivating that case, compares only to the NeSymReS base, and uses a large amount of mechanically extracted ground-truth structure.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The defensible novelty is the first well-demonstrated prompt-like control interface for an amortized numerical-to-expression Transformer across several heterogeneous structural hint types, not the first use of prior knowledge in symbolic regression. Its enduring insight is architectural and interaction-oriented. By 2026, LLM-SR, DrSR, PG-SR, and LLM-PySR broaden prior expression, reflection, robustness, and executable checking, so a modern extension should focus on uncertain human hypotheses, hard verification, modular post-training hint registration, and compute-matched comparisons rather than repeating oracle-conditioned accuracy gains.

reviewer_notes: Read all 15 pages of the official ICML 2023 PMLR final, including appendices A-D. Visually inspected Figure 1, all main result Figures 2-6, Tables 1-2, and Appendix Figures 7-11 from the cached PDF; numerical descriptions use only values legible in those figures or printed in Table 1. The current competitive audit used primary arXiv and OpenReview records checked on 2026-08-23 and includes the uncited 2020 prior-knowledge predecessor plus 2026 prior-guided and language-model search-control methods. The additive-constant distribution is reported exactly as printed and flagged as a likely ambiguity rather than silently corrected. This is a primary full-text pass, not an independent secondary verification.
